payload.baseline:
Four elements, black-box described, taken directly from the winner's clustering - nothing redrawn.

E1 THE MILESTONE LANE (in engine/gate.ts, on the bless path). Black box: given a blessed gate on a worktree-resident iteration, it leaves that iteration's work as a commit on the iteration's own branch and the working tree clean. Says nothing about trunk. Carries F1.

E2 THE POINTER WRITER (also on the bless path, deliberately a separate element). Black box: given a grant being recorded, it stamps the tag name under which that grant's evidence will be reachable. Depends on nothing existing yet, because the tag name is deterministic. Carries F8.

E3 THE ATOMIC CLOSE (in engine/worktree.ts, shipMerge). Black box: given an iteration to close, it either produces a trunk commit carrying that iteration's live claims - with two parents, a created tag, and the events withheld but reachable - or it changes nothing at all and says why. Carries F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, F9.

E4 THE WORKING PLACE (in engine/worktree.ts, provisionWorktree). Black box: given a new iteration, it yields a worktree that can run its own checks, and warns if it would fork from a state that does not match what is running. Carries F11, F12.

Plus one standing constraint, not an element: F13 (protect the record from erasure) is enforced at the git invocation layer over every element.

F10 (keep ended work visible) is allocated to the EXISTING grant index rather than to a new element - it is satisfied by not moving grants.jsonl, which is se.adr-grant-index-stays-on-trunk. Recorded explicitly so the column is not read as unallocated.
payload.allocation_exact: Every function is allocated exactly once, with no function split across two elements and no element claiming a function twice. F1 -> E1. F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, F9 -> E3. F8 -> E2. F10 -> the grant index (existing, unchanged). F11, F12 -> E4. F13 -> the standing constraint. Thirteen functions, thirteen allocations. The one that could have been double-allocated is F9 (refuse on doubt): E1 and E4 also have failure paths, but their failures are ordinary errors, not the atomicity guarantee - only E3 must guarantee that a failure leaves trunk byte-identical, so F9 sits there alone.
payload.interfaces_both_ends:
Three interfaces, each declared at both ends.

I1 E2 -> E3, the TAG NAME. Declared by E2 as the value it stamps onto a grant, and by E3 as the tag it must create. Symmetric because both ends derive it from the same deterministic rule (iter/<id>), so neither has to ask the other. This is the only cross-cluster coupling in the design.

I2 E1 -> E3, the BRANCH STATE. Declared by E1 as the commits it leaves on the branch, and by E3 as what it counts when deciding whether the branch is empty. Asymmetric on purpose and in one direction only: E3 reads what E1 wrote, and E3's refusal must never write back - that is what keeps a refused close from undoing committed milestones.

I3 E4 -> E1/E3, the WORKING PLACE. Declared by E4 as the worktree and branch it provisions, and by both E1 and E3 as the place they operate on. Symmetric in naming: all three use the same branch name and worktree path rule.

No interface is declared at only one end, and no element reaches inside another - E1 and E3 share the branch, not each other's internals.
